areas.title: Verification and oversight
areas.question: What can a less capable overseer reliably verify about a more capable AI’s properties, answers, and actions without reproducing all of the system’s work?
areas.description: A useful verification method must state which claims it can check, put bounds on how often it can be wrong, and set reasonable bounds on the resources its verifier needs. In mathematics, there are exact definitions of correct and incorrect statements and what constitutes a proof. For the open-ended answers generated by modern AI systems in many other fields, we need to define anew what counts as sufficient evidence and how to evaluate it before letting the system take action.

areas.title: Control and delegation
areas.question: What authority can we delegate to AI while preserving our ability to intervene as AI becomes more intelligent than us?
areas.description: Explore protocols that make the scope of a delegated task explicit: which tools may be used, which actions require approval, and when execution should stop. Guarantees should account for the environment and the power of the user, not just the AI model.

areas.title: Composition
areas.question: Which safety properties can be better achieved when connections between models, tools, and agents are limited?
areas.description: A property established for one component may fail when it interacts with another. Study interfaces, shared resources, patterns of interaction, and assumptions under which local guarantees support a claim about an entire system, as well as constructions that show when composition is impossible.

areas.title: Shaping multi-agent dynamics
areas.question: How should we design agents and structure their interactions to build safe multi-agent systems with provable guarantees?
areas.description: Behavior of an AI system often emerges from complex interactions between many agents (swarms). These agents cooperate, compete, assume roles, and communicate to further their individual or shared goals. Though swarms of agents have emerged only recently, the problem of constraining and shaping the dynamics of interacting parties is well studied in other settings. We draw on ideas from game theory, distributed computing, social psychology, and law to govern these dynamics and achieve desirable outcomes.

areas.title: Formal verification
areas.question: How can formal verification enable powerful AI throughout software development without creating new risks of cyberattacks or otherwise dangerous behavior?
areas.description: Develop mathematical proofs that the software surrounding AI enforces safety constraints, including containment that holds regardless of a model’s internal decisions. The scope extends from securing conventional computing infrastructure to verifying the hardware and software that run deep learning, and ultimately to systems that repeatedly improve themselves. Alongside these technical problems, study how to organize and equip researchers to produce the necessary proofs before the risks materialize.

areas.title: Impossibility as a safety result
areas.question: What limits on technologically achievable safety guarantees can be proved, and how can those limits inform which laws, policies, and regulations must be adopted?
areas.description: Not all safety goals are achievable, and sometimes provably so. Understanding these limits can help policymakers identify requirements that cannot be satisfied together, justify imposing restrictions, and clarify what access auditors need to assess safety claims.

areas.title: Leveraging AI for AI safety research
areas.question: How can we use AI to develop new AI safety concepts, definitions, insights, and formal guarantees?
areas.description: As AI grows smarter, it gains a greater capacity to act in unanticipated ways and to cause harm despite human safeguards. For humans to keep pace, we must use AI wisely as a tool to improve and accelerate AI safety research. This includes exploring whether recent developments in AI-assisted mathematics can accelerate the creation of mathematical foundations for AI safety.

areas.title: Incentives and institutions
areas.question: How should incentives work alongside technical safeguards?
areas.description: Technical mechanisms operate within organizations, markets, and legal institutions. Model those interactions and assess which guarantees remain useful when the people and systems involved have different objectives, and under what assumptions.

areas.title: Cryptography and security
areas.question: How do we repurpose cryptographic tools for secrecy, authentication, multi-party secure computation and obfuscation to navigate the AI multi-agentic world?
areas.description: Cryptography studies how parties can compute and communicate securely even when some behave maliciously. For AI agents, we need to model agents capabilities and adversary agents completely differently to protect users. Each traditional cryptographic goal requires a new precise model of the adversary's computational power, information, and ability to collude as well as a proof of security.

areas.title: Legal alignment
areas.question: How can legal constructs be leveraged to develop technical methods for building safe by design superintelligence?
areas.description: Explore how the law’s concepts, principles, and institutions can serve as a blueprint to propose technical methods for robustly safe AI systems -- and develop theoretical and empirical case studies of such legal alignment.

areas.title: Attribution
areas.question: Can we attribute model decisions to training data?
areas.description: The map from training data or information in large contexts can be opaque. Tools for disentangling the effects of these kinds of information on the behavior of AIs could serve as essential tools for interpretability and safety, but at present, all such tools are heuristic and unverifiable. If we want to fully understand AI behavior, we need reliable and rigorous ways to trace model decisions and outputs back to data.
